summary:
This run covered 8 evals; 2 were skipped as not applicable (should_trigger: false cases — "workload-not-identified-no-premature-binding" and "non-llm-outage-must-not-trigger" — both variants triggered correctly at 100% there, consistent with the "must not trigger" expectation being satisfied). Of the remaining 6 evals, 2 ("incident-signature-match" and "third-party-model-boundary-disclosed") had trigger_fired at 0/1, meaning the behavior under test never actually fired for either variant in those scenarios, so no expected-output or assertion data could be collected (all marked null/inconclusive) — these are gaps in the measurement, not a performance comparison.

For the 4 evals where data exists for with_skill, with_skill has assertion-level results (ranging 67%-100% pass rates across 4-6 assertions per eval) and non-zero runtimes/costs (roughly 33s-1m14s, $0.28-$0.62). However, without_skill shows "0s" runtime and "$0.00" cost with null assertion data in 3 of these 4 evals ("transient-vs-config-verdict", "agent-loop-on-lambda-binding", "self-hosted-model-locus-not-provider"), suggesting without_skill's run either did not execute, was not captured, or produced no scorable output in those cases — this looks like missing data for without_skill rather than a measured weaker performance.

The one eval with a direct head-to-head on assertions, "telemetry-readiness-gap," shows a clear contrast: with_skill passed all 4 assertions (100%) while without_skill failed all 4 (0%), covering identifying missing telemetry, explaining why gaps block diagnosis, citing a telemetry check-id (both via LLM judge and regex check). Variant_a also met the expected output here while without_skill did not. Variant_b took longer (1m43s vs 1m14s) and cost more ($0.86 vs $0.62) in this eval, so the longer/costlier run did not correspond to higher measured quality in this instance.

Expected-output pass rates otherwise: with_skill met expectations in 2 of the 4 non-skipped, non-missing-trigger evals ("transient-vs-config-verdict" at 100% with high confidence, and "telemetry-readiness-gap" at 100% with medium confidence), and failed to meet expectations in "agent-loop-on-lambda-binding" and "self-hosted-model-locus-not-provider" (0%, high/medium confidence). Variant_b failed to meet expected output in every eval where it has data (0% across the board), though confidence levels for these without_skill misses are often unspecified or not reported as high, so some of these findings should be read with caution.

No quality-comparison pairs were evaluated for any eval (all marked pairs_skipped: 1, zero comparable pairs), so there is no direct side-by-side quality judgment available anywhere in this run. Output consistency across repeated runs is also null throughout — no consistency data was captured for either variant in any eval.

Overall, the data that exists points to with_skill having more complete, scorable outputs and assertion passes where comparisons were possible, and the one clean head-to-head (telemetry-readiness-gap) favors with_skill on both assertions and expected output. However, a large portion of this run is missing or inconclusive data for without_skill (null assertions, 0s/0$ metrics in several evals) and for both variants in two evals where the trigger never fired, which limits how much can be concluded. Treat these findings as partial: the measurement coverage itself, especially for without_skill, is incomplete rather than indicating poor performance.

transient-vs-config-verdict.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task. The trigger behavior under test fired successfully (1/1), but data beyond that is very one-sided: without_skill produced no usable output at all for this task — it has a 0% expected-output pass rate, zero runtime, and zero cost, suggesting it did not actually run or generate a response for this case (metrics show 0s/$0.00). Because of that, almost no comparative data exists: assertion-level results, quality comparisons, and output-consistency checks could not be computed for without_skill (all marked null or skipped), and the quality comparison explicitly shows 0 pairs evaluated with 1 pair skipped.

Variant_b did produce a response and met the expected output (1/1, with high confidence). On the 6 individual assertions checked against with_skill, it passed 4 of 6 (67%): it successfully named an explicit fault locus, presented the finding as a structured ruling with supporting evidence, reported what it observed per signal (including absence of data), and correctly avoided prescribing customer-side config changes for a provider-side issue. It failed two assertions: it did not report the server-error rate across multiple models (only the one the user mentioned), and it did not include a catalog check-id in its findings — these are concrete gaps in the response's completeness that a single pass/fail aggregate would hide.

Since without_skill has no corresponding assertion, quality, or consistency data, no side-by-side comparison on cost, runtime, or quality can be made — with_skill's runtime (~1m8s) and cost (~$0.57) are not matched against any real activity from without_skill. Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was not available for either variant. Overall, this result set reflects an incomplete run for without_skill rather than a substantive quality comparison between the two variants; the only solid findings are about with_skill's own behavior on this task, where it met the core expected output but left two specific assertions unmet.

telemetry-readiness-gap.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task. The trigger behavior under test fired successfully (1/1), confirming the scenario was exercised as intended.

On expected-output match, with_skill met the expected output (1/1, 100%, medium confidence) while without_skill did not (0/1, 0%, high confidence). The confidence rating for without_skill's failure is high, meaning that non-match is a fairly reliable measurement, whereas with_skill's pass is based on only medium confidence, so it should be read as a fairly solid but not maximally certain result.

At the assertion level, all 4 assertions were evaluated for both variants, and every single one followed the same pattern: with_skill passed and without_skill failed. These assertions check for (1) identifying specific missing telemetry rather than vague advice, (2) explaining why each gap blocks diagnosis, (3) citing an LLM-TEL check id via LLM judgment, and (4) citing a telemetry check-id via regex (a more objective, pattern-based check). The fact that both an LLM-based and a regex-based assertion independently agree on the same pass/fail split adds some confidence that this is a real, consistent difference in this task rather than an artifact of one evaluator. However, this is a single task with a small number of assertions, so the finding shouldn't be generalized broadly without more data.

On runtime and cost, with_skill was faster (1m14s vs 1m43s, ~29s less) and cheaper ($0.62 vs $0.86) than without_skill. Context window utilization was low for both (6.5% vs 4.8%), with no compaction events for either, indicating neither variant strained context limits.

The quality comparison and output-consistency dimensions were not usable here: quality had 0 pairs evaluated (1 pair skipped), and output consistency is null for both variants, so no data exists on run-to-run stability or relative output quality beyond the assertion checks.

Overall, for this single task, with_skill met the expected output and all assertions while without_skill did not, and with_skill was also faster and lower-cost. Since quality-comparison and consistency data are absent, and this rests on one task instance, this should be viewed as a notable but narrow signal rather than a broad verdict on either variant.

agent-loop-on-lambda-binding.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task, and the data available for the two variants is very asymmetric, so direct comparison is limited.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior-under-test trigger fired (1/1). On the "expected output" check, both with_skill and without_skill failed to meet it (0/1 each). For with_skill this failure is reported with high confidence (i.e., the measurement itself is trustworthy), while without_skill's result has no confidence annotation provided, so its failure is reported but with no stated reliability.

Assertions: Detailed per-assertion results are only available for with_skill (without_skill shows null throughout, meaning this data wasn't captured/applicable for it, not that it failed). Variant_a passed 4 of 5 assertions (80%):
- It passed assertions on stating the hosting binding explicitly and not conflating the agent loop with AgentCore, distinguishing the model-call stage from the Lambda compute stage, treating Lambda/ALB as stages outside model-path checks, and naming the hosting binding (regex-based) — all passed with high confidence (except one judged on pattern basis).
- It failed one assertion: noting that the Lambda platform error metric can't separate client from server errors (or declining to rule on it) — this failed with medium confidence.
Since without_skill has no assertion data, no side-by-side comparison on these specific checks is possible; this is an area where the eval could not evaluate both sides equally.

Metrics: with_skill had a measured runtime of ~68s and a cost of $0.57, with low context window utilization (6.4%) and no compaction. without_skill shows 0s runtime and $0.00 cost, which likely indicates it did not run or produce a comparable trace for this task rather than being more efficient — this should be treated as missing data, not a performance advantage. Context utilization for without_skill (4.3%) is also present despite the 0s/$0 figures, reinforcing that the metrics are incomplete or inconsistent for this variant in this eval.

Quality comparison: No quality pairs were evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 pair skipped), so there is no direct quality comparison between the two variants for this task.

Consistency: No output consistency data is available for either variant (both null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall: The only clearly comparable, high-confidence finding is that both variants failed to meet the expected output on this task. Beyond that, the data is predominantly one-sided (assertions and runtime/cost only meaningfully populated for with_skill) or missing (quality comparison, consistency), so this single eval does not support a meaningful head-to-head judgment between with_skill and without_skill beyond noting their shared failure on the expected-output check.

Trigger/setup: The behavior-under-test fired successfully (1/1).

Expected output: Both with_skill and without_skill failed to meet the expected output (0/1 each). For with_skill this judgment carries medium confidence; for without_skill confidence isn't reported. Since both failed, this dimension does not differentiate them — it points to a shared shortfall (or a possible issue with how the expected output was specified) rather than one variant underperforming the other.

Assertions: Detailed per-assertion results exist only for with_skill (4/5 passed, 80%), while without_skill has no assertion data at all (marked null/inconclusive on every assertion). This means no real assertion-level comparison could be made — we only know how with_skill did in isolation. Within with_skill's results, it passed checks on treating provider health as not-applicable, avoiding Bedrock-specific failover suggestions, binding error signals to load balancer/application metrics, and avoiding a Bedrock namespace for a self-hosted model. It failed the assertion checking whether the locus was correctly classified as INFRASTRUCTURE rather than PROVIDER (high confidence failure). Since without_skill has no corresponding data, we cannot say whether it would have passed or failed these same checks.

Metrics: with_skill took ~33s and cost ~$0.28, with 5.5% context window utilization; without_skill shows 0s runtime and $0.00 cost, with slightly lower 4.4% utilization. The zero runtime/cost for without_skill is unusual and suggests it may not have actually executed or its metrics weren't captured, rather than reflecting a genuinely faster/cheaper run — this should be treated as missing/inconclusive data rather than a real efficiency advantage.

Quality comparison: No quality pairs were evaluated (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no basis to compare output quality between the variants.

Output consistency: No consistency data is available for either variant (both null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed.

Overall state: This is a thin, largely one-sided dataset. The only dimension with real detail (assertions) only covers with_skill, and without_skill lacks assertion, quality, and consistency data entirely, with metrics that look like they may be placeholders/missing rather than true zeros. The one dimension measured for both (expected output) shows both failing, which is not a point of differentiation but a shared gap. No meaningful comparative conclusion between with_skill and without_skill can be drawn from this evaluation as structured; most apparent differences reflect missing data for without_skill rather than demonstrated performance differences.
